Yes — very likely.

At your time and location:

- The Moon is **9.1° above the horizon**, so it is genuinely above the geometric horizon, though still fairly low. That is about the width of a clenched fist held at arm’s length.
- Its azimuth of **109°** places it roughly **east-southeast**.
- It is **91% illuminated**, so it is a bright waxing/waning gibbous Moon and should be conspicuous once you look in the right direction.
- The Sun is **16° below the horizon**, during astronomical twilight. The sky will still have some residual glow near the western/northwestern sunset side, but your Moon is in the opposite, eastern part of the sky and should stand out well.
- Clear skies and normal unaided eyesight are more than sufficient.

The main limitation is the low altitude: buildings, hills, haze, dust, or a blocked eastern-southeastern horizon could hide it. If you have a reasonably open view toward **ESE**, look about **9° up** and you should be able to see it easily—probably as a bright, obvious gibbous disk rather than needing to search carefully.
